reasoning.Student A:
My goal is to maximize my value. The schools offer values of w=$64, x=$63, y=$76, and z=$77. Therefore, I prefer z and y over w and x. Between z and y, I prefer z because it has a higher value ($77 > $76). Between w and x, I prefer w since it has a higher value ($64 > $63).

However, priority also matters. I have priority 1 at w and y, and priority 2 at x and z. Since most applicants favor y > x > w > z, y will be very competitive. I need to assess if my high priority at y is enough to overcome the strong preference of other applicants. Similarly, z will be less competitive because most applicants rank it last.

Given that my priority at y is 1, and its value is high ($76), it is likely my best option. z has the highest value ($77) but I only have priority 2. The other applicants ranking y > x > w > z suggests they will likely apply to y first. If I also apply to y first, I might get matched there due to my priority 1.

If I am rejected from y, I will automatically be considered at my next choice. Since z has the highest value, it should be my second choice. Even though I have priority 2 at z, the fact that most applicants rank it last increases my chances.

If I am rejected from both y and z, I will be considered at w and x. I have priority 1 at w and priority 2 at x. Since I value w more than x, I will rank w third and x last.

Therefore, my ranking should be y > z > w > x.
